title: Limited Authority
description: Negotiating as if you cannot decide alone buys time and room.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: A negotiator who must check with someone else cannot be pushed to a final yes on the spot. Limited authority is a shield: it slows the pace and forces the other side to make their best case first.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: If you cannot sign, pressure to decide now has nothing to grip. It also softens concessions, since "I'll have to see if that's possible" is not a refusal.

sections.title: Real-Life Examples
content: "I'll need to run this past my partner."
A buyer who says the final number is above what they are authorised to approve.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: Decisions deferred to an absent authority.
Offers that can only be recommended, not accepted.

sections.title: How to Use It
sections.content: Be honest about who decides. Use the pause to gather information and avoid committing under pressure.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: Authority claimed as an excuse to avoid ever deciding.
A "final approver" who is never available.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
content: Ask early who can actually sign the deal.
If authority is limited, get their best offer before they leave.

sections.title: Mistakes People Make
content: Assuming you must decide on the spot.
Letting an invisible approver stall indefinitely.

sections.title: Key Lessons
content: Not being able to sign is a shield.
It removes the pressure of an instant yes.
